Blown
blone
v. (past participle of blow; in the Authorized Version chiefly of the trumpet sounded in war, in worship, and at the great ingathering)
From Old English blawan, to blow. The Hebrew at Amos 3:6 is taqa, to thrust or drive, and so to blow a trumpet by driving breath through it; at Isaiah 27:13 the noun is shophar, the ram's-horn trumpet.

Biblical Definition

A trumpet blown in an Israelite city was never a neutral sound. Amos makes the point with two rhetorical questions that carry his whole doctrine of providence: “Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?” (Amos 3:6). The first question is obvious — of course the alarm frightens them — and it is set there to make the second unavoidable. Ezekiel shows the alarm sounded to an army that will not come: “They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof” (Ezekiel 7:14). Nothing is wrong with the trumpet; the paralysis is judicial. Isaiah gives the great and hopeful use: “in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown, and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the LORD in the holy mount at Jerusalem” (Isaiah 27:13). The trumpet that gathers the perishing and the outcast is the one the New Testament takes up at the last trump. Job supplies a stranger use: “a fire not blown shall consume him” (Job 20:26) — a fire no man kindled and no bellows fed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives blown as the participle of blow, and defines the sounding of a wind instrument by forcing breath through it.

expand to see more

BLOWN, pp. Driven by wind; fanned; sounded by blowing.

BLOW, v.t. To throw or drive a current of air upon; to fan.

2. To sound a wind instrument; as, blow the trumpet.

3. To drive by a current of air; to impel.

TRUMPET, n. A wind instrument of music, used chiefly in war and military exercises.

Key Scripture

Amos 3:6 — "Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?"

Isaiah 27:13 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown, and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the LORD in the holy mount at Jerusalem."

Ezekiel 7:14 — "They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof."

Job 20:26 — "All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle."

Modern Corruption

Amos 3:6 is softened until God is no longer the author of calamity, which is precisely the claim the prophet is making.

expand to see more

Amos 3:6 is among the most avoided verses in the English Bible, and the avoidance takes several forms — that evil here means only calamity and therefore the verse says less than it appears to; that the LORD merely permits rather than does; that the prophet is speaking loosely. The first observation is correct and does not help: the Hebrew ra is indeed calamity rather than moral wickedness, and the question is precisely whether God is the author of calamity. Amos says He is. Isaiah says the same in the first person: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things. The 1689 Confession holds the line without making God the author of sin, distinguishing His holy decree from the sinful means creatures freely employ — a distinction the Scripture itself makes when Joseph tells his brothers that they thought evil and God meant it unto good.

The reason the doctrine matters is that the alternative is worse. A God who does not govern calamity is a God who cannot answer prayer about it, cannot promise that all things work together for good, and cannot be trusted in the dark. Amos's rhetorical structure is the pastor's ally, not his enemy: the alarm is sounded so that the city may fear and repent, and the God who raised the trouble is the God who may be sought. Isaiah 27:13 is where the trumpet finally leads — the perishing and the outcast gathered to worship in the holy mount.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew taqa, to thrust, to blow a trumpet — Amos 3:6, Ezekiel 7:14; shophar, the ram's horn — Isaiah 27:13; nephach, to blow or fan — Job 20:26.

expand to see more

Hebrew taqa — to drive or thrust, and so to blow a horn; Amos 3:6 and Ezekiel 7:14.

Hebrew shophar — the ram's-horn trumpet; Isaiah 27:13, “the great trumpet.”

Hebrew chatsotserah — the silver trumpet of the priests; Numbers 10:2, the other instrument.

Hebrew nephach — to breathe or fan; Job 20:26, of a fire no man kindled.

Hebrew ra — evil in the sense of calamity; the disputed word at Amos 3:6.

Usage

"“Shall a trumpet be blown… and the people not be afraid?” — the obvious question set before the hard one."

"“They have blown the trumpet… but none goeth to the battle” — a judicial paralysis."

"“The great trumpet shall be blown” — the perishing and the outcast gathered."
